raw_case_text:
In 2015, a 4-year and 6-month-old boy was admitted to our hospital for recurrent lung infections and hematuria for more than 2 years. Physical examination on admission revealed visible tonsils; cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymphadenectasis; dry rales in his both lungs; no murmurs in the heart; abdominal softness, no hepatosplenomegaly; no positive signs on nervous system. He had a BCG vaccination at birth with no adverse effects. Epstein-Barr (EB) virus IgM and cytomegalovirus (CMV) IgM were detected. High titers of anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) for PR3 were detected (see  Table 1 ). Chest CT showed pulmonary nodules with cavity formation, bronchiectasis, and patchy infiltration. Bilateral maxillary and ethmoid sinusitis were also seen in paranasal sinuses CT ( Figures 1A, B ). Ultrasound suggested the enlargement of liver, spleen, and superficial lymph nodes. Urine routine revealed increased urine red blood cells. Renal biopsy pathology indicated slight glomerular lesions ( Figure 1C ). Lymph node biopsy only demonstrated reactive hyperplasia. Bronchoscopy revealed no obvious abnormalities. Lung biopsy suggested an uneven distribution of lesions, and infiltrations of lymphocytes around the bronchiole with hyperplasia of collagen fibers ( Figure 2 ). Bone marrow aspiration indicates hyperplasia of granulocytes.
The boy was diagnosed as GPA based on upper airway, lung, and kidney involvements, and positive ANCA (refer to EULAR/PRINTO/PRES criteria). He was treated with oral prednisone at the initial dose of 1 mg/kg/day, tapered to 0.2 mg/kg/day by month 6, and 0.15 mg/kg/day as maintenance therapy. At the same time, he was given monthly intravenous cyclophosphamide infusion at the dose of 500mg/m2 for 6 months, and then mycophenolate mofetil was started as maintenance therapy. His hematuria improved. However, he still experienced recurrent lung infections within 2 years of follow-ups, and repeated bronchoscopy showed mucosal nodules. This patient was suspected of having lymphoproliferative disease and accepted genetic testing with the consent of his mother (his father not available). A mutation E1021K (c.3061 G >A) in the PIK3CD gene was found in this boy, while his mother had no mutation. He was then diagnosed with APDS1 and received regular immunoglobulin (400 mg/kg/month) and rapamycin treatment with the improvements of lung infection and hematuria. Considering his pulmonary infections, he was treated with piperacillin and Tazobactam, and then received Trimethoprim/Sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis for 6 months.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 4-year-6-month-old boy presented in 2015 with a >2-year history of recurrent lower respiratory tract infections and persistent hematuria.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Experiencing recurrent pulmonary infections and hematuria for over 2 years, the child was initially diagnosed with PR3-ANCA-positive granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) and treated with oral prednisone, 6 monthly infusions of IV cyclophosphamide (500 mg/m2), and maintenance mycophenolate mofetil, which improved his hematuria. However, recurrent lung infections persisted over the next 2 years with new endobronchial mucosal nodules on repeat bronchoscopy, prompting genetic testing for an underlying primary immunodeficiency.
subjective.past_medical_history: 2-year history of recurrent pulmonary infections and hematuria; received BCG vaccination at birth without adverse effects.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for >2 years of recurrent lung infections, cough, sinusitis, and hematuria.

objective.physical_examination: Visible tonsillar hypertrophy; cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymphadenopathy; bilateral dry pulmonary rales on auscultation; soft abdomen without palpable hepatosplenomegaly; normal cardiac and neurological examinations.
objective.routine_investigations: Urinalysis showed microscopic hematuria (increased urine RBCs). Positive serum Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) IgM and cytomegalovirus (CMV) IgM antibodies; high-titer anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies against proteinase-3 (PR3-ANCA). Abdominal and superficial ultrasound demonstrated hepatosplenomegaly and generalized superficial lymphadenopathy.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT showed cavitating pulmonary nodules, bronchiectasis, and patchy infiltrates; paranasal sinus CT showed bilateral maxillary and ethmoid sinusitis. Initial bronchoscopy was normal, while repeat bronchoscopy during 2-year follow-up revealed endobronchial mucosal nodules. Renal biopsy showed mild glomerular lesions; lymph node biopsy showed reactive hyperplasia; bone marrow aspiration showed granulocytic hyperplasia; lung biopsy demonstrated patchy peribronchiolar lymphocytic infiltration with collagen fiber hyperplasia. Genetic sequencing identified a de novo heterozygous gain-of-function mutation in PIK3CD: c.3061G>A (p.E1021K; absent in his mother).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive genetic diagnosis of Activated PI3K-Delta Syndrome Type 1 (APDS1; confirmed by heterozygous PIK3CD c.3061G>A [p.E1021K] mutation) initially mimicking PR3-ANCA-positive granulomatosis with polyangiitis (cavitating lung nodules, bronchiectasis, pansinusitis, hematuria) with positive EBV IgM and CMV IgM serologies and lymphoproliferation. After incomplete control of recurrent pulmonary infections on GPA regimens (prednisone, IV cyclophosphamide, and mycophenolate mofetil), targeted therapy with monthly intravenous immunoglobulin replacement (400 mg/kg/month), oral sirolimus (rapamycin), piperacillin-tazobactam, and 6 months of prophylactic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole led to sustained resolution of both pulmonary infections and hematuria.
